extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy; social reformers and general readers interested in economic justice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the concluding normative and explanatory principles Henry George advances about poverty, land, progress, and the relation of economic and moral law in Progress and Poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gains from increased productive power are appropriated by land owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever benefit would accrue from increased productive power (more fertility, inventions like steam and electricity) would be but temporary because land, being private property, the classes that now monopolize the bounty of the Creator would monopolize all the new bounty: 'Land owners would alone be benefited. Rents would increase, but wages would still tend to the starvation point!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: harnessing steam, telegraphy, iron and steel machinery — these increases in productive power have historically resulted in landlords capturing the gains rather than raising wages or lightening toil. The passage is used as empirical and theoretical evidence that merely increasing material productive power will not relieve poverty so long as land remains privately monopolized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poverty springs from social injustice and monopolization, not immutable natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The want and suffering of civilization do not follow from the laws of nature or inevitable population pressures but from 'the ignorance and selfishness of men in refusing to conform to natural laws' — poverty is the product of unjust social institutions (especially land monopoly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit rejection of deterministic or Malthusian explanations for poverty. The author argues that social arrangements (property in land, distribution mechanisms) cause waste and suffering that could be prevented by just institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properly understood Political Economy is hopeful and shows poverty is unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Economy, when 'freed' from misinterpretation and shackles, is 'radiant with hope' and demonstrates that a social state in which poverty is unknown is possible: 'the laws which govern the production and distribution of wealth show that the want and injustice of the present social state are not necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book positions its economic analysis as normative and emancipatory: correct understanding of economic laws implies remedies (institutional changes) that can eliminate poverty. This contrasts with the 'dismal' presentation of Political Economy as hopeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic law and moral law harmonize; justice is integral to social prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws discovered by Political Economy 'harmonize with what seems to be the law of mental development' and 'social law runs into and conforms with the moral law'; moral and economic truths converge: justice infallibly brings reward and injustice its punishment (in social life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This claim underpins normative prescriptions: policy and institutional design should follow both economic and moral principles because they are essentially one. The argument is used to justify social reforms aimed at justice (especially land reforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human will and institutions determine aggregate human condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking men in the aggregate, their condition is as they make it: 'human will is the great factor' in social development; social conditions are governed by law but shaped by human choices and institutions rather than by immutable fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports an activist reform orientation: because human will and institutional arrangement matter, deliberate changes (legal, political) can improve distribution and abolish unnecessary suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population does not necessarily outrun subsistence; Malthusian doctrines are false
rubrics_metrics.description: The author claims to have 'seen that population does not tend to outrun subsistence' and that the doctrines asserting overpopulation as the source of misery are fallacious. Increases in population, coupled with improvements in the arts, can increase wealth rather than produce inevitable scarcity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct repudiation of Malthusian theory; the text points to historical and theoretical evidence (treated earlier in the book) to show that alleged natural population limits do not justify existing inequality or the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private ownership of land is the root of social enslavement and aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Private property in land leads to monopoly, aristocracy, serfdom, and the enslavement of laborers ('their enslavement the ultimate result of private property in land'). Legal titles to land are called absurd when they deprive the many of rightful use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this diagnosis follows advocacy for abolishing or radically reforming private land ownership (see referenced chapters on making land common property and effects of that change). The argument is both moral and economic: private land ownership misallocates the Creator's bounty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolishing rent capture or resuming land values will not injure laborers and will relieve poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied across the conclusion and indexed material: reforms that confiscate or tax rent (or have government resume the increase in land values) will not hurt the masses and are proposed as remedies; the 'land owners... will not be injured by confiscation of rent' and the recovery of land values by government is discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although detailed mechanisms are in other chapters, the conclusion reiterates that redirecting land-generated unearned wealth (rent) away from private hands is both just and practicable and is central to eliminating poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress is institutional, not a change in human nature; civilization can retrograde
rubrics_metrics.description: Human progress 'is not the improvement of human nature' but consists in changes in the constitution of society; these advances are not fixed and may be lost—civilization may decline unless based on justice: 'to endure must be based on justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reframes policy goals: securing progress requires stable just institutions (land tenure, political arrangements). The warning of possible retrogression underscores urgency for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: The laws visible in society imply unseen continuities; individual life's apparent injustices do not negate ultimate moral order
rubrics_metrics.description: Although individual life often seems purposeless or unjust, the author argues we do not see the whole of individual life; social laws show justice ultimately prevailing even if individuals cannot perceive the whole orbit: 'we shall not say that the law which is manifest in social life is not true of individual life' — rather, our view is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This philosophical claim supports moral consolation and perseverance among reformers: apparent lack of individual justice does not undermine the science's ethical foundations nor the case for pursuing justice in institutions.
